claim: N. cinerea isolate CCUG346T (346T) encodes a single locus containing homologues of all 13 components necessary for a functional T6SS.
source: We identified a single locus in N. cinerea isolate CCUG346T (346T) (https://www.ccug.se/strain?id=346) that encodes homologues of all 13 components that are necessary for a functional T6SS (Cascales and Cambillau, 2012), including genes predicted to encode canonical T6SS components Hcp and VgrG (Figure 1A and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis of the genome sequence and reference to established T6SS components.

claim: Six putative effector and immunity gene pairs (nte and nti) were identified in N. cinerea 346T using T6SS-effector prediction software.
source: We used T6SS-effector prediction software tools (Li et al., 2015) to search for putative effectors. In total we identified six putative effector and immunity genes, termed nte and nti for Neisseria T6SS effector/immunity, respectively.
evidence: The claim is based on computational prediction using specialized software and is supported by citation to the prediction tool.

claim: All predicted T6SS-related orfs and Nte/Ntis in N. cinerea 346T are encoded on a 108,141 bp plasmid.
source: Of note, all predicted T6SS-related orfs and Nte/Ntis in N. cinerea 346T were found to be encoded on a 108,141 bp plasmid, revealed by PacBio sequencing, and confirmed by PCR and sequencing.
evidence: The claim is supported by whole genome sequencing data (PacBio) and confirmed by PCR and sequencing experiments, as shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Nte/Nti 1–5 are encoded adjacent to the structural gene cluster, with Nte6/Nti6 encoded elsewhere in the plasmid.
source: Nte/Nti 1–5 are encoded adjacent to the structural gene cluster, with Nte6/Nti6 encoded elsewhere in the plasmid (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the plasmid map shown in Figure 1B and confirmed by PCR analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Hcp was detected in both whole cell lysates and supernatants from wild-type N. cinerea 346T but not in the ΔT6SS mutant.
source: As expected, Hcp was detected in both fractions from the wild-type strain but not in the negative control strain (ΔT6SS mutant) (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Hcp was present in cell lysates from the ΔtssB mutant but not detected in cell supernatants.
source: Importantly, Hcp was present in cell lysates from the ΔtssB mutant, but not detected in cell supernatants, while Hcp secretion was restored by complementation of the ΔtssB mutant by chromosomal expression of TssB with a C-terminal sfGFP fusion (ΔtssB::tssB-sfGFP) (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 1C demonstrating differential Hcp localization in the mutant versus complemented strain.

claim: Hcp secretion was restored by complementation of the ΔtssB mutant with chromosomal expression of TssB-sfGFP fusion.
source: Importantly, Hcp was present in cell lysates from the ΔtssB mutant, but not detected in cell supernatants, while Hcp secretion was restored by complementation of the ΔtssB mutant by chromosomal expression of TssB with a C-terminal sfGFP fusion (ΔtssB::tssB-sfGFP) (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data in Figure 1C showing Hcp in supernatants of the complemented strain.

claim: The survival of N. cinerea 27178A was reduced by around an order of magnitude following incubation with N. cinerea 346T compared with the ΔT6SS mutant.
source: The survival of N. cinerea 27178A was reduced by around an order of magnitude following incubation with N. cinerea 346T compared with the ΔT6SS mutant (Figure 1D), confirming that the N. cinerea 346T T6SS is active during inter-bacterial competition.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative competition assay data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The N. cinerea 346T T6SS is active during inter-bacterial competition.
source: The survival of N. cinerea 27178A was reduced by around an order of magnitude following incubation with N. cinerea 346T compared with the ΔT6SS mutant (Figure 1D), confirming that the N. cinerea 346T T6SS is active during inter-bacterial competition.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the competition assay results showing T6SS-dependent killing.

claim: Time-lapse microscopy revealed dynamic T6SS foci inside N. cinerea 346TΔtssB::tssB-sfGFP bacteria, with structures extending/contracting over seconds.
source: Time-lapse microscopy revealed dynamic T6SS foci inside bacteria, with structures extending/contracting over seconds (Figure 2A and Figure 2—video 1) consistent with T6SS activity (Gerc et al., 2015; Ringel et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 2A and video, and is consistent with published observations of T6SS dynamics.

claim: Deletion of tssM in strain 346TΔtssB::tssB-sfGFP abolished T6SS activity.
source: To further confirm T6SS activity, we deleted the gene encoding the TssM homologue in strain 346TΔtssB::tssB-sfGFP, abolishing T6SS activity (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and confirmed that in the absence of TssM, fluorescent structures were rarely seen (< 5% of cells in the ΔtssM background, compared with > 60% in the strain expressing TssM; Figure 2C and Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data in Figure 2B and quantification in Figure 2C, as well as competition assay data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the absence of TssM, fluorescent T6SS structures were rarely seen (< 5% of cells) compared with > 60% in the strain expressing TssM.
source: To further confirm T6SS activity, we deleted the gene encoding the TssM homologue in strain 346TΔtssB::tssB-sfGFP, abolishing T6SS activity (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and confirmed that in the absence of TssM, fluorescent structures were rarely seen (< 5% of cells in the ΔtssM background, compared with > 60% in the strain expressing TssM; Figure 2C and Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of fluorescent foci shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Increased SYTOX staining of prey cells was detected immediately adjacent to predator bacteria displaying T6SS activity.
source: Interestingly, we detected increased SYTOX staining of prey cells immediately adjacent to predator bacteria displaying T6SS activity (Figure 3 and Figure 3—video 1), indicating that the N. cinerea T6SS induces cell damage and lysis of its prey.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data showing SYTOX Blue staining in Figure 3.

claim: The N. cinerea T6SS induces cell damage and lysis of its prey.
source: Interestingly, we detected increased SYTOX staining of prey cells immediately adjacent to predator bacteria displaying T6SS activity (Figure 3 and Figure 3—video 1), indicating that the N. cinerea T6SS induces cell damage and lysis of its prey.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the SYTOX staining data which indicates membrane permeabilization and cell lysis.

claim: All Ntes contain a conserved Rhs domain and a C-terminal region with predicted activities previously described in T6SS effectors.
source: As shown in Figure 4, all Ntes contain a conserved Rhs domain, frequently associated with polymorphic toxins (Busby et al., 2013), and a C-terminal region with predicted activities previously described in T6SS effectors (Alcoforado Diniz et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 4 and references to published work on Rhs domains and T6SS effectors.

claim: Nte1 contains an N-terminal PAAR motif and C-terminal phospholipase domain (cd00618).
source: Nte1 contains an N-terminal PAAR motif, which can associate with the VgrG tip of the T6SS (Shneider et al., 2013) and C-terminal phospholipase domain (cd00618).
evidence: The claim is supported by domain analysis shown in Figure 4 and citation to work on PAAR domains.

claim: Nte2 contains an N-terminal PAAR domain and has a predicted RNase domain (pfam15606) in its C-terminal region.
source: Nte2 also contains an N-terminal PAAR domain and has a predicted RNase domain (pfam15606) in its C-terminal region.
evidence: The claim is supported by domain analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Nte3 is a putative endonuclease of the HNH/Endo VII family with conserved LHH (pfam14411).
source: Nte3 is a putative endonuclease of the HNH/Endo VII family with conserved LHH (pfam14411).
evidence: The claim is supported by domain analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Nte4 contains a GIY-YIG nuclease domain (cd00719).
source: Nte4 contains a GIY-YIG nuclease domain (cd00719) and Nte5 is predicted to be an HNH/endo VII nuclease with conserved AHH (pfam14412), with Nte6 predicted to contain an HNHc endonuclease active site (cd00085).
evidence: The claim is supported by domain analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Nte5 is predicted to be an HNH/endo VII nuclease with conserved AHH (pfam14412).
source: Nte4 contains a GIY-YIG nuclease domain (cd00719) and Nte5 is predicted to be an HNH/endo VII nuclease with conserved AHH (pfam14412), with Nte6 predicted to contain an HNHc endonuclease active site (cd00085).
evidence: The claim is supported by domain analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Nte6 is predicted to contain an HNHc endonuclease active site (cd00085).
source: Nte4 contains a GIY-YIG nuclease domain (cd00719) and Nte5 is predicted to be an HNH/endo VII nuclease with conserved AHH (pfam14412), with Nte6 predicted to contain an HNHc endonuclease active site (cd00085).
evidence: The claim is supported by domain analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: All Ntes are toxic when expressed in E. coli, leading to decreased viability and reduced optical density compared to empty vector controls.
source: All Ntes are toxic, with their expression leading to decreased viability and reduced optical density (OD) of E. coli cultures compared to empty vector controls; toxicity was counteracted by co-expression of the corresponding Nti.
evidence: The claim is supported by growth curves and CFU data shown in Figure 5A-F.

claim: Toxicity of Ntes was counteracted by co-expression of the corresponding Nti in E. coli.
source: All Ntes are toxic, with their expression leading to decreased viability and reduced optical density (OD) of E. coli cultures compared to empty vector controls; toxicity was counteracted by co-expression of the corresponding Nti.
evidence: The claim is supported by growth curves and CFU data shown in Figure 5A-F demonstrating rescue of toxicity by immunity proteins.

claim: N. cinerea 346T caused between a 50- to 100-fold decrease in survival of N. meningitidis compared with the ΔT6SS strain, irrespective of lineage or serogroup.
source: N. cinerea 346T caused between a 50- to 100-fold decrease in survival of the meningococcus compared with the ΔT6SS strain, irrespective of lineage or serogroup (Figure 6A) and an approximately fivefold reduction in survival of the gonococcus (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by competition assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: N. cinerea 346T caused an approximately fivefold reduction in survival of N. gonorrhoeae.
source: N. cinerea 346T caused between a 50- to 100-fold decrease in survival of the meningococcus compared with the ΔT6SS strain, irrespective of lineage or serogroup (Figure 6A) and an approximately fivefold reduction in survival of the gonococcus (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by competition assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The meningococcal capsule protects bacteria against T6SS attack.
source: Using a capsule-null strain (ΔsiaD) in competition assays with wild-type N. cinerea 346T or the T6SS mutant, we found reduced survival of the unencapsulated mutant compared to the wild-type (Figure 6C). Therefore, the meningococcal capsule protects bacteria against T6SS attack.
evidence: The claim is supported by competition assay data comparing encapsulated and unencapsulated strains shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Non-piliated prey strain segregates to the periphery of the colony and escapes T6SS-mediated assault, dominating the expanding colony.
source: As expected based on previous observations of Tfp-mediated cell sorting in Neisseria (Oldewurtel et al., 2015; Zöllner et al., 2017), the non-piliated prey strain (346TΔnte/i3-5ΔpilE1/2_sfCherry; red) segregates to the periphery of the colony, in this location the prey strain escapes T6SS-mediated assault and dominates the expanding colony (Figure 7A and Figure 7—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 7A and video, and is consistent with published observations of Tfp-mediated sorting.

claim: When the prey is piliated, pilus-mediated cell interactions prevent displacement of cells to the expanding front, so the susceptible strain is outcompeted by the T6SS+ strain.
source: In contrast, when the prey is piliated, pilus-mediated cell interactions prevent displacement of cells to the expanding front (Oldewurtel et al., 2015; Pönisch et al., 2018; Zöllner et al., 2017), so the susceptible strain (Tfp-expressing 346TΔnte/i3-5_sfCherry Tfp+, red) is outcompeted by the T6SS+ strain (Tfp-expressing 346T_sfGfp Tfp+, green) (Figure 7B and Figure 7—video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 7B and video, and references to published work on Tfp-mediated interactions.

claim: When both strains are piliated and immune to T6SS attack, there is no dominance of either strain.
source: When both strains are piliated and immune to T6SS attack, there is no dominance of either strain (Figure 7C and Figure 7—video 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 7C and video.

claim: The piliation status of the prey impacts survival against T6SS.
source: Assessment of the relative recovery of piliated and non-piliated prey in competition assays also supported the observation that the piliation status of the prey impacts survival against T6SS (Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by competition assay data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Tfp influence the outcome of T6SS-mediated antagonism through structuring and partitioning bacteria in mixed microcolonies.
source: These results highlight that Tfp influence the outcome of T6SS-mediated antagonism through structuring and partitioning bacteria in mixed microcolonies.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined microscopy and competition assay data showing differential outcomes based on piliation status.

claim: Enhanced prey survival is due to segregation of the non-piliated prey from the piliated attacker, allowing the prey to achieve a favourable position for outgrowth at the edge of the colony.
source: These data support the idea that the enhanced prey survival is due to segregation of the non-piliated prey from the piliated attacker, allowing the prey to achieve a favourable position for outgrowth at the edge of the colony.
evidence: The claim is inferred from competition assay data in Figure 8A showing that prey survival is enhanced only when prey is non-piliated, combined with microscopy observations of spatial segregation.

claim: Reduction in prey survival was equivalent whether both or neither the attacker and prey express Tfp.
source: Moreover, prey survival was equivalent when attacker and prey either both have, or both lack Tfp (Figure 8A and Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by competition assay data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Tfp are not required for T6SS activity.
source: Reduction in prey survival was equivalent whether both or neither the attacker and prey express Tfp, demonstrating that Tfp are not required for T6SS activity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that T6SS-mediated killing occurs regardless of whether both strains have or lack Tfp.

claim: The N. cinerea T6SS is encoded on a plasmid.
source: Here, we provide the first description of a functional T6SS in Neisseria spp. We show that the N. cinerea T6SS is encoded on a plasmid and antagonises pathogenic relatives, N. meningitidis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
evidence: The claim is supported by PacBio sequencing data and PCR confirmation shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The N. cinerea T6SS antagonises pathogenic relatives N. meningitidis and N. gonorrhoeae.
source: Here, we provide the first description of a functional T6SS in Neisseria spp. We show that the N. cinerea T6SS is encoded on a plasmid and antagonises pathogenic relatives, N. meningitidis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
evidence: The claim is supported by competition assay data shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: Pilus expression by a prey strain enhances susceptibility to T6SS compared to a non-piliated prey, by preventing segregation from a T6SS-wielding attacker.
source: We explored the impact of Tfp on N. cinerea T6SS-dependent killing within a colony and show that pilus expression by a prey strain enhances susceptibility to T6SS compared to a non-piliated prey, by preventing segregation from a T6SS-wielding attacker.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy and competition assay data shown in Figure 7.

claim: N. cinerea is a commensal of the human respiratory tract.
source: In Neisseria species, including Neisseria cinerea a commensal of the human respiratory tract, interbacterial contacts are mediated by Type four pili (Tfp) which promote formation of aggregates and govern the spatial dynamics of growing Neisseria microcolonies.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about N. cinerea ecology.

claim: Type four pili (Tfp) mediate interbacterial contacts in Neisseria species.
source: In Neisseria species, including Neisseria cinerea a commensal of the human respiratory tract, interbacterial contacts are mediated by Type four pili (Tfp) which promote formation of aggregates and govern the spatial dynamics of growing Neisseria microcolonies.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about Tfp function in Neisseria.

claim: Type four pili promote formation of aggregates in Neisseria species.
source: In Neisseria species, including Neisseria cinerea a commensal of the human respiratory tract, interbacterial contacts are mediated by Type four pili (Tfp) which promote formation of aggregates and govern the spatial dynamics of growing Neisseria microcolonies.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about Tfp function in Neisseria.

claim: Type four pili govern the spatial dynamics of growing Neisseria microcolonies.
source: In Neisseria species, including Neisseria cinerea a commensal of the human respiratory tract, interbacterial contacts are mediated by Type four pili (Tfp) which promote formation of aggregates and govern the spatial dynamics of growing Neisseria microcolonies.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about Tfp function in Neisseria.

claim: The human microbiota is critical for the development of a healthy gastrointestinal immune system.
source: The human microbiota is critical for the development of a healthy gastrointestinal immune system (Round and Mazmanian, 2009; Sommer and Bäckhed, 2013) and can also protect the host from invasion by pathogenic bacteria (Kamada et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The human microbiota can protect the host from invasion by pathogenic bacteria.
source: The human microbiota is critical for the development of a healthy gastrointestinal immune system (Round and Mazmanian, 2009; Sommer and Bäckhed, 2013) and can also protect the host from invasion by pathogenic bacteria (Kamada et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The Type VI Secretion System (T6SS) provides an effective strategy to eliminate competitors in a contact-dependent manner.
source: One mechanism, the Type VI Secretion System (T6SS), provides an effective strategy to eliminate competitors in a contact-dependent manner and is widespread in Gram negative bacteria from many different environments (Coulthurst, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: T6SS is widespread in Gram negative bacteria from many different environments.
source: One mechanism, the Type VI Secretion System (T6SS), provides an effective strategy to eliminate competitors in a contact-dependent manner and is widespread in Gram negative bacteria from many different environments (Coulthurst, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The T6SS is a contractile, bacteriophage-like nanomachine that delivers toxins into target organisms.
source: The T6SS is a contractile, bacteriophage-like nanomachine that delivers toxins into target organisms (Cianfanelli et al., 2016; Ho et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: T6SS-associated effectors possess a broad range of activities, including nucleases, phospholipases, peptidoglycan hydrolases, and pore-forming proteins.
source: T6SS-associated effectors possess a broad range of activities, including nucleases (Koskiniemi et al., 2013; Ma et al., 2014; Pissaridou et al., 2018), phospholipases (Flaugnatti et al., 2016; Russell et al., 2013), peptidoglycan hydrolases (Whitney et al., 2013), and pore-forming proteins (Mariano et al., 2019); each effector is associated with a cognate immunity protein to prevent self-intoxication and to protect against kin cells (Alcoforado Diniz et al., 2015; Unterweger et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Each T6SS effector is associated with a cognate immunity protein to prevent self-intoxication and to protect against kin cells.
source: T6SS-associated effectors possess a broad range of activities, including nucleases (Koskiniemi et al., 2013; Ma et al., 2014; Pissaridou et al., 2018), phospholipases (Flaugnatti et al., 2016; Russell et al., 2013), peptidoglycan hydrolases (Whitney et al., 2013), and pore-forming proteins (Mariano et al., 2019); each effector is associated with a cognate immunity protein to prevent self-intoxication and to protect against kin cells (Alcoforado Diniz et al., 2015; Unterweger et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The impact of the T6SS in pathogenesis and bacterial competition has been established in vitro and in some cases in vivo in pathogens such as Pseudomonas, Vibrio, Salmonella, and Shigella.
source: In pathogens such as Pseudomonas, Vibrio, Salmonella, and Shigella, the impact of the T6SS in pathogenesis and bacterial competition has been established in vitro and in some cases in vivo (Anderson et al., 2017; Sana et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Commensal bacteria harbour T6SSs.
source: Commensal bacteria also harbour T6SSs, although how these systems combat pathogens has only been elucidated for Bacteroidetes in the intestinal tract (Russell et al., 2014); further studies are needed to gain a greater appreciation of how T6SSs in commensals influence microbial communities and pathogens in other niches.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: How T6SSs in commensals combat pathogens has only been elucidated for Bacteroidetes in the intestinal tract.
source: Commensal bacteria also harbour T6SSs, although how these systems combat pathogens has only been elucidated for Bacteroidetes in the intestinal tract (Russell et al., 2014); further studies are needed to gain a greater appreciation of how T6SSs in commensals influence microbial communities and pathogens in other niches.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The human nasopharynx hosts a polymicrobial community.
source: The human nasopharynx hosts a polymicrobial community (Kumpitsch et al., 2019; Cleary and Clarke, 2017; Ramos-Sevillano et al., 2019), which can include the obligate human pathogen Neisseria meningitidis, as well as related but generally non-pathogenic, commensal Neisseria species (Diallo et al., 2016; Dorey et al., 2019; Gold et al., 1978; Knapp and Hook, 1988; Sheikhi et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The human nasopharynx can include the obligate human pathogen Neisseria meningitidis, as well as related but generally non-pathogenic, commensal Neisseria species.
source: The human nasopharynx hosts a polymicrobial community (Kumpitsch et al., 2019; Cleary and Clarke, 2017; Ramos-Sevillano et al., 2019), which can include the obligate human pathogen Neisseria meningitidis, as well as related but generally non-pathogenic, commensal Neisseria species (Diallo et al., 2016; Dorey et al., 2019; Gold et al., 1978; Knapp and Hook, 1988; Sheikhi et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In vivo studies have demonstrated an inverse relationship between carriage of commensal Neisseria lactamica and N. meningitidis.
source: In vivo studies have demonstrated an inverse relationship between carriage of commensal Neisseria lactamica and N. meningitidis (Deasy et al., 2015), whereas in vitro studies have revealed that some commensal Neisseria demonstrate potentially antagonistic effects against their pathogenic relatives (Custodio et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: In vitro studies have revealed that some commensal Neisseria demonstrate potentially antagonistic effects against their pathogenic relatives.
source: In vivo studies have demonstrated an inverse relationship between carriage of commensal Neisseria lactamica and N. meningitidis (Deasy et al., 2015), whereas in vitro studies have revealed that some commensal Neisseria demonstrate potentially antagonistic effects against their pathogenic relatives (Custodio et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Commensal and pathogenic Neisseria species have been shown to interact closely in mixed populations.
source: Commensal and pathogenic Neisseria species have also been shown to interact closely in mixed populations (Custodio et al., 2020; Higashi et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Type IV pili enable pathogenic Neisseria to adhere to host cells.
source: These filamentous organelles enable pathogenic Neisseria to adhere to host cells (Nassif et al., 1993; Virji et al., 1991) and are crucial for microbe-microbe interactions and the formation of bacterial aggregates and microcolonies (Helaine et al., 2007; Higashi et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Type IV pili are crucial for microbe-microbe interactions and the formation of bacterial aggregates and microcolonies in Neisseria.
source: These filamentous organelles enable pathogenic Neisseria to adhere to host cells (Nassif et al., 1993; Virji et al., 1991) and are crucial for microbe-microbe interactions and the formation of bacterial aggregates and microcolonies (Helaine et al., 2007; Higashi et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Tfp interactions can dictate bacterial positioning within a community.
source: In addition, Tfp interactions can dictate bacterial positioning within a community; non-piliated strains have been shown to be excluded to the expanding edge of colonies growing on solid media (Oldewurtel et al., 2015; Zöllner et al., 2017) while heterogeneity in pili, for example through post translational modifications, can alter how cells integrate into microcolonies (Zöllner et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Non-piliated strains have been shown to be excluded to the expanding edge of colonies growing on solid media.
source: In addition, Tfp interactions can dictate bacterial positioning within a community; non-piliated strains have been shown to be excluded to the expanding edge of colonies growing on solid media (Oldewurtel et al., 2015; Zöllner et al., 2017) while heterogeneity in pili, for example through post translational modifications, can alter how cells integrate into microcolonies (Zöllner et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Heterogeneity in pili can alter how cells integrate into microcolonies.
source: In addition, Tfp interactions can dictate bacterial positioning within a community; non-piliated strains have been shown to be excluded to the expanding edge of colonies growing on solid media (Oldewurtel et al., 2015; Zöllner et al., 2017) while heterogeneity in pili, for example through post translational modifications, can alter how cells integrate into microcolonies (Zöllner et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: N. cinerea expresses Tfp that promote microcolony formation.
source: This species expresses Tfp that promote microcolony formation, can closely interact with N. meningitidis in a Tfp-dependent manner and impairs meningococcal association with human epithelial cells (Custodio et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: N. cinerea can closely interact with N. meningitidis in a Tfp-dependent manner.
source: This species expresses Tfp that promote microcolony formation, can closely interact with N. meningitidis in a Tfp-dependent manner and impairs meningococcal association with human epithelial cells (Custodio et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: N. cinerea impairs meningococcal association with human epithelial cells.
source: This species expresses Tfp that promote microcolony formation, can closely interact with N. meningitidis in a Tfp-dependent manner and impairs meningococcal association with human epithelial cells (Custodio et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: T6SS genes have been identified in other Neisseria spp. isolated from human throat swab cultures.
source: Similarly, T6SS genes have been recently identified in other Neisseria spp. isolated from human throat swab cultures (Calder et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: This study provides the first description of a functional T6SS in Neisseria spp.
source: Here, we provide the first description of a functional T6SS in Neisseria spp.
evidence: The claim is based on the novelty of the findings presented in this manuscript.

claim: Contraction of the T6SS leads to Hcp secretion, a hallmark of a functional T6SS.
source: Contraction of the T6SS leads to Hcp secretion, a hallmark of a functional T6SS (Cascales and Cambillau, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature establishing Hcp secretion as a marker of T6SS function.

claim: TssB is a component of the T6SS-tail-sheath required for contraction.
source: Therefore, to establish whether the N. cinerea T6SS is functional, we assessed Hcp levels in whole cell lysates and supernatants from wild-type N. cinerea and a ΔtssB mutant, based on previous work demonstrating that TssB is a component of the T6SS-tail-sheath required for contraction (Brackmann et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: N. cinerea 27178A lacks a T6SS and Nte/Nti pairs identified in N. cinerea 346T.
source: Next, we performed competition assays between N. cinerea 346T or the ΔT6SS mutant against N. cinerea 27178A which lacks a T6SS and Nte/Nti pairs identified in N. cinerea 346T.
evidence: The claim is based on genomic analysis of the strain.

claim: Strain 346TΔtssB::tssB-sfGFP exhibits comparable T6SS killing as wild-type N. cinerea 346T.
source: We further analysed the activity of the T6SS by visualising assembly and contraction in N. cinerea 346TΔtssB::tssB-sfGFP; this strain exhibits comparable T6SS killing as wild-type N. cinerea 346T (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by competition assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The N. cinerea T6SS appears to be constitutively active.
source: Examination of N. cinerea T6SS activity revealed several interesting features. Microscopy demonstrated that T6SS attack (tit-for-tat) is not required to provoke firing of the system. Instead, the T6SS appears to be constitutively active in N. cinerea (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is inferred from microscopy data showing T6SS activity in the absence of prey attack.

claim: The N. cinerea T6SS is capable of inducing lysis of prey bacteria.
source: Furthermore, the system is capable of inducing lysis of prey bacteria (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by SYTOX Blue staining data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Lysis of prey bacteria could be mediated by Nte1 which harbours a putative phospholipase domain in the C-terminus.
source: Of the six Ntes we identified, lysis could be mediated by Nte1 which harbours a putative phospholipase domain in the C-terminus.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the predicted domain structure of Nte1.

claim: A combination of effectors might be needed to elicit prey lysis.
source: Alternatively, a combination of effectors might be needed to elicit prey lysis.
evidence: The claim is speculative.

claim: Polysaccharide capsules are largely thought to provide bacteria with a strategy for evading host immune killing.
source: Polysaccharide capsules are largely thought to provide bacteria with a strategy for evading host immune killing (Lewis and Ram, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The meningococcal capsule has an alternative role in defence against other bacteria.
source: Here, we found that the meningococcal capsule has an alternative role in defence against other bacteria.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the competition assay data showing enhanced susceptibility of capsule-null mutants.

claim: The extracellular polysaccharide of V. cholerae and the colanic acid capsule of E. coli confer defence against T6SS attack.
source: Similar findings have been reported for other bacteria; for example, the extracellular polysaccharide of V. cholerae and the colanic acid capsule of E. coli confer defence against T6SS attack (Hersch et al., 2020; Toska et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The capsule may sterically impair the ability of the T6SS to penetrate the target cell membrane, and/or inhibit access of T6SS effectors to their cellular targets.
source: One potential mechanism is that the capsule sterically impairs the ability of the T6SS to penetrate the target cell membrane, and/or inhibits access of T6SS effectors to their cellular targets.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a potential mechanism.

claim: Some commensal Neisseria species have capacity to produce polysaccharide capsules.
source: Interestingly, recent genetic evidence indicates that some commensal Neisseria species also have capacity to produce polysaccharide capsules (Clemence et al., 2018), which might also confer a survival advantage in mixed populations that include strains expressing T6SS.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Polysaccharide capsules in commensal Neisseria might confer a survival advantage in mixed populations that include strains expressing T6SS.
source: Interestingly, recent genetic evidence indicates that some commensal Neisseria species also have capacity to produce polysaccharide capsules (Clemence et al., 2018), which might also confer a survival advantage in mixed populations that include strains expressing T6SS.
evidence: The claim is speculative, extrapolating from the findings about meningococcal capsule.

claim: T6SS-mediated killing requires intimate association with prey.
source: Although T6SS-mediated killing can be advantageous to a producing strain during bacterial competition, this requires intimate association with its prey (MacIntyre et al., 2010; Russell et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: One way for susceptible bacteria to evade T6SS killing is to avoid direct contact with attacking cells.
source: Thus, one way for susceptible bacteria to evade T6SS killing is to avoid direct contact with attacking cells (Borenstein et al., 2015; Smith et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The Tfp is a key mediator of interbacterial and interspecies interactions in Neisseria.
source: In Neisseria, the Tfp is a key mediator of interbacterial and interspecies interactions (Custodio et al., 2020; Higashi et al., 2011) and pilus-mediated interactions influence the spatial structure of a growing community (Oldewurtel et al., 2015; Zöllner et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Pilus-mediated interactions influence the spatial structure of a growing Neisseria community.
source: In Neisseria, the Tfp is a key mediator of interbacterial and interspecies interactions (Custodio et al., 2020; Higashi et al., 2011) and pilus-mediated interactions influence the spatial structure of a growing community (Oldewurtel et al., 2015; Zöllner et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In N. gonorrhoeae, non-piliated bacteria segregate to the expanding front of the colony.
source: In N. gonorrhoeae, non-piliated bacteria segregate to the expanding front of the colony and Tfp-mediated spatial reorganisation can allow bacteria to avoid external stresses or strains competing for resources (Oldewurtel et al., 2015; Zöllner et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Tfp-mediated spatial reorganisation can allow bacteria to avoid external stresses or strains competing for resources.
source: In N. gonorrhoeae, non-piliated bacteria segregate to the expanding front of the colony and Tfp-mediated spatial reorganisation can allow bacteria to avoid external stresses or strains competing for resources (Oldewurtel et al., 2015; Zöllner et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Physical exclusion driven by Tfp-loss or modification could be an effective strategy to evade and survive an antagonistic interaction.
source: We predicted that this would be especially relevant in the context of T6SS-mediated antagonism. For example, physical exclusion driven by Tfp-loss or modification could be an effective strategy to evade and survive an antagonistic interaction, while pilus-mediated interactions might be less favourable for a susceptible prey.
evidence: The claim is a prediction based on prior knowledge of Tfp-mediated sorting.

claim: Pilus-mediated interactions might be less favourable for a susceptible prey in the context of T6SS-mediated antagonism.
source: We predicted that this would be especially relevant in the context of T6SS-mediated antagonism. For example, physical exclusion driven by Tfp-loss or modification could be an effective strategy to evade and survive an antagonistic interaction, while pilus-mediated interactions might be less favourable for a susceptible prey.
evidence: The claim is a prediction based on prior knowledge of Tfp-mediated interactions.

claim: Tfp loss may occur naturally in a polymicrobial environment and is an established phenomenon in pathogenic Neisseria.
source: Importantly, Tfp loss may occur naturally in a polymicrobial environment and is an established phenomenon in pathogenic Neisseria (Hagblom et al., 1985; Helm and Seifert, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Many bacteria that employ T6SSs for inter-bacterial competition also express Tfp.
source: It is noteworthy that many bacteria (e.g. Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Vibrio cholerae, Acinetobacter baumannii, enteropathogenic E. coli) that employ T6SSs for inter-bacterial competition also express Tfp.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about bacterial species that possess both T6SS and Tfp.

claim: The findings are of broad relevance for the impact of contact-dependent killing.
source: Therefore, our findings are of broad relevance for the impact of contact-dependent killing, and further emphasise how precise spatial relationships can have profound effects on how antagonistic and mutualistic factors combine to influence the development of microbial communities.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the significance of the findings.

claim: Precise spatial relationships can have profound effects on how antagonistic and mutualistic factors combine to influence the development of microbial communities.
source: Therefore, our findings are of broad relevance for the impact of contact-dependent killing, and further emphasise how precise spatial relationships can have profound effects on how antagonistic and mutualistic factors combine to influence the development of microbial communities.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the broader implications of the findings.

claim: To date, plasmid encoded T6SSs have only been described in Campylobacter species.
source: To date, plasmid encoded T6SSs have only been described in Campylobacter species (Marasini and Fakhr, 2016), with this plasmid T6SS mobilised via conjugation (Marasini et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The Campylobacter plasmid T6SS is mobilised via conjugation.
source: To date, plasmid encoded T6SSs have only been described in Campylobacter species (Marasini and Fakhr, 2016), with this plasmid T6SS mobilised via conjugation (Marasini et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Other small plasmids have been reported in N. cinerea.
source: Although other small plasmids have been reported in N. cinerea (Knapp et al., 1984; Roberts, 1989) and N. cinerea can be a recipient of N. gonorrhoeae plasmids (Genco et al., 1984), it is not yet known whether T6SS plasmids are widespread among Neisseria, or whether the plasmid can be mobilised by conjugation or transformation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: N. cinerea can be a recipient of N. gonorrhoeae plasmids.
source: Although other small plasmids have been reported in N. cinerea (Knapp et al., 1984; Roberts, 1989) and N. cinerea can be a recipient of N. gonorrhoeae plasmids (Genco et al., 1984), it is not yet known whether T6SS plasmids are widespread among Neisseria, or whether the plasmid can be mobilised by conjugation or transformation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: It is not yet known whether T6SS plasmids are widespread among Neisseria.
source: Although other small plasmids have been reported in N. cinerea (Knapp et al., 1984; Roberts, 1989) and N. cinerea can be a recipient of N. gonorrhoeae plasmids (Genco et al., 1984), it is not yet known whether T6SS plasmids are widespread among Neisseria, or whether the plasmid can be mobilised by conjugation or transformation.
evidence: The claim acknowledges a gap in current knowledge.

claim: It is not yet known whether the N. cinerea T6SS plasmid can be mobilised by conjugation or transformation.
source: Although other small plasmids have been reported in N. cinerea (Knapp et al., 1984; Roberts, 1989) and N. cinerea can be a recipient of N. gonorrhoeae plasmids (Genco et al., 1984), it is not yet known whether T6SS plasmids are widespread among Neisseria, or whether the plasmid can be mobilised by conjugation or transformation.
evidence: The claim acknowledges a gap in current knowledge.

claim: In Acinetobacter baylyi, T6SS-induced prey cell lysis contributes to acquisition of plasmids from target cells.
source: Interestingly, in Acinetobacter baylyi, T6SS-induced prey cell lysis contributes to acquisition of plasmids from target cells (Ringel et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Six genes encoding putative effectors were identified based on their proximity to the T6SS locus, their pairwise arrangement with genes encoding proteins with homology to immunity proteins and the presence of conserved domains.
source: In total six genes encoding putative effectors were identified based on their proximity to the T6SS locus, their pairwise arrangement with genes encoding proteins with homology to immunity proteins and the presence of conserved domains such as PAAR and Rhs domains in the predicted proteins (Alcoforado Diniz et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on bioinformatic analysis and established criteria for identifying T6SS effectors.

claim: Nte3, 4, 5, and 6 may be cargo effectors while Nte1 and Nte2 are more typical of specialised or evolved effectors with integral PAAR domains at their N-termini.
source: Our bioinformatic predictions suggest Nte3, 4, 5, and 6 may be cargo effectors while Nte1 and Nte2 are more typical of specialised or evolved effectors with integral PAAR domains at their N-termini (Durand et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on bioinformatic predictions and citation to published work on PAAR-containing effectors.

claim: nte5 may represent an orphan Rhs-CT.
source: Of note nte5 encodes a protein with a shorter Rhs domain compared to the other five putative effectors (319AA compared to 695-735AA), raising the possibility that this may represent an orphan Rhs-CT, as described in other genomes (Kirchberger et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on comparison of domain sizes and citation to published work on orphan Rhs-CT.

claim: Hcp or VgrG could be responsible for delivery of effectors encoded nearby in the T6SS locus.
source: Based on previous work, Hcp, or VgrG could be responsible for delivery of effectors encoded nearby in the T6SS locus (Hachani et al., 2014), with or without the involvement of the adjacent DUF2169 family protein (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from published work on T6SS effector delivery mechanisms.

claim: Nte/Nti6 may not be associated with the T6SS.
source: As nte/nti6 are not part of the T6SS locus and are encoded elsewhere on the plasmid, Nte/Nti6 may not be associated with the T6SS.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the genomic location of nte/nti6.

claim: Additional experimentation will be needed to confirm the contributions of Nte1-6 to T6SS activity and killing, and to demonstrate direct secretion via the T6SS.
source: Thus, although our bioinformatic analysis and protein expression in E. coli suggests Nte1-6 as effectors, additional experimentation will be needed to further confirm their contributions to T6SS activity and killing, and to demonstrate direct secretion via the T6SS.
evidence: The claim acknowledges limitations of the current study and the need for further experiments.
